title: A son on the other side of the world wants to send a dementia Christmas greeting. No call, no app, no time zones.
meta_title: Dementia Christmas: Video Message From Family | CareStreamAI
meta_description: A son abroad records a Christmas greeting on a private link. You approve it, staff play it at a good moment, and a reminder invites another.
lede: Christmas is when families who live far away feel the distance most. For a dementia Christmas in a care home, a son's voice can matter more than a card. CareStream gives him a private link to record a short greeting, holds it for your approval, and lets staff play it at a good moment. It sits alongside the rest of your training and knowledge tools.

intro.heading: He cannot fly home. He wants her to hear him on the day.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: Daniel lives in Perth and has not seen his mother, Mrs Wilkes, for two years. She moved into the home in the spring. He rings on Sundays, but the hours do not line up and calls are hard for her to follow. At Christmas he wants to say more than a card can. He offers to send a clip to the activities lead's phone. She would love to say yes, but she knows she should not keep recordings of residents on a personal phone.

trail.text: Mrs Wilkes settles. Her key worker records the family details.
Daniel asks how he can be part of Christmas from Perth.
The activities lead puts up the tree and plans the day.
There is no safe way to receive his clip.
He sends a message on a personal phone instead. It is not approved.
Nobody can find the clip in the hubbub of the day.
Daniel asks if she heard it. Nobody is sure.
“How do you involve relatives who live far away?” A card on a shelf is all you have.

trail_close: The family wanted to be there. The gap is between a loving offer and a safe way to receive, check and play it. Here is how CareStream closes it, step by step.

why.heading: Why a voice from far away matters at Christmas
why.sub: Distance is hard for families, and the day carries a lot of feeling.

cards.title: Voices carry what cards cannot
cards.body: Many teams build a dementia Christmas around familiar songs, decorations and talk of past years. A greeting in a son's own voice adds something personal. It is one gentle part of the day, not a promise about how anyone will feel.

cards.title: Family views count
cards.body: Under section 4 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005, a person's past and present wishes and feelings are considered, and so are the views of people interested in their welfare. Care must also reflect preferences.

cards.title: Privacy still applies on a festive day
cards.body: Regulation 10 includes ensuring privacy. A greeting on a staff phone is a risk. One a manager approved, played from a private link on the home's own device, is safer.

how.heading: From Perth to the lounge, step by step.
how.sub: Video messages and reminders are part of the resident profiles feature, in the same system as your policies and training. They are on Professional and above. See how staff use resident knowledge too.

blocks.heading: Daniel records on his phone, with no app or account

He can add a short title and remove a clip before pressing Send. The upload shows progress and can resume after a lost signal
It is not a call, so time zones do not matter. He records when it suits him, and it waits

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: Does the family need an app or an account?
items.a: No. They open a private link in the email on their phone, record or choose a video, add a short title and press Send. A manager checks it before staff see it.
No. It is not a call. Daniel records when he likes, and the clip waits for your approval and for the right moment on your side.

items.q: How long can a greeting be?
items.a: Up to 60 seconds each, with up to 5 videos per link and up to 150MB per upload. It is converted so it plays on any phone, tablet or computer.

items.q: Can staff play it before I have checked it?
items.a: No. Every family video waits for a manager to preview and approve it. A manager can edit the title and add a note first.

items.q: How does a carer find it on the day?
items.a: They open the This is me chat in the Staff Hub and ask. Approved videos appear under the answer with the resident's name and room number. The chat reads the title and note, never the clip.
We do not claim that. A voice may spark a smile or talk about past Christmases, or it may not. It is one gentle option, and the carer chooses the moment and judges how it goes.

items.q: Can the family be reminded to send another?
items.a: Yes. A manager can switch on gentle email reminders for a contact. They stop after 3 with no reply, and each email has a stop link. The default is off.

items.q: Which plan is it on, and can I try it?
items.a: Resident profiles, photos, videos and reminders are on Professional and above. There is a 14 day free trial, and the pricing page shows which plan includes it. You can create an account or book a demo first.

limits.heading: Honest limits: a recorded greeting, not a call

cards.title: A recording, not a visit
cards.body: A greeting is a recording that staff play when they choose. It does not replace a visit, a phone call or your own Christmas plans, and it is only as good as the moment the carer picks.

cards.title: The chat reads titles, not clips
cards.body: The chat cannot watch a video or describe what is in it, so a vague title is hard to find. The hub shows up to 10 newest videos per resident.

cards.title: Nothing is promised for the person
cards.body: CareStream does not diagnose or treat. It does not claim a message will calm or cheer anyone. The carer chooses the moment, stops if it upsets, and follows the care plan.

faqs.heading: Christmas, family video and the hub, answered

items.q: How can I plan a dementia Christmas in a care home?
items.a: Keep the day familiar and unhurried, involve family where you can, and follow each person's care plan. A video from family is one gentle part. Your dementia awareness training covers how to read how someone is feeling.

items.q: What is a reminiscence box, and can a video go in one?
items.a: A reminiscence box is a physical collection of objects, photos and keepsakes that prompt memories and conversation. A video message is a digital companion to it. Approved photos can appear in the chat too, found by caption.

items.q: How can family help with dementia memory?
items.a: Family hold the stories, names and voices. A short message, or a photo with a caption, gives staff something personal to talk about. It supports the person, but it does not change their dementia memory.

items.q: Where do I note what to record about a person?
items.a: See our guide to the this is me document.

items.q: Does a manager approve a video before staff can play it?
items.a: Yes. A family video stays hidden until a manager approves it. Videos a manager adds are approved at once.
Yes. A manager can turn them off, and each email has a Stop these reminders link. Reminders stop at once if the person moves on or dies.

items.q: What does the law say about preferences and privacy?
items.a: Regulation 9 says care must meet needs and reflect preferences, and regulation 10 includes ensuring privacy. Check your own policies for recordings.

guide.heading: How to make a family greeting work on the day
guide.lede: A little planning in November makes the difference in December. Here is a simple run of events.

sections.h3: Invite early, and say what you need
paragraphs: Email families in November, and tell them the clip should be under a minute and that the home checks it first. A relaxed voice and a short story work better than a long speech. Encourage them to mention the person by name.
Your reminiscence box, the photos on the wall and the songs you play are all part of the day. The greeting joins them. Link it with the person's profile so staff know the names in it.

sections.h3: Choose the moment on the day
paragraphs: Christmas can be busy and loud. Many people do better in a quiet corner, so pick a calm moment, sit beside the person and keep the sound gentle. Stop if they are upset, and note how it went.
checklist: Is the clip approved and titled so staff can find it?
Is the tablet charged and the sound gentle?
Have you chosen a calm moment and a quiet corner?
Will you tell the family afterwards that it was played?

sections.h3: Keep the door open for the new year
paragraphs: A thank you tells a relative their effort was used. If they have said they would like to send more, switch on a gentle reminder from the Family tab. See resident knowledge for the wider picture.

guide.note: This page describes how the software works and is not legal or clinical advice. Follow each resident's care plan and your own policies for how you use recordings.
